title: IPC looking into apparent Germany protest at Russian skiers on Paralympic podium
content:
The International Paralympic Committee is looking into an apparent protest by two German athletes while on the podium when the Russian anthem was played at the Winter Paralympics.

Russian athlete Anastasiia Bagiian, guided by Sergei Siniakin, won gold in the visually impaired classification of the women’s cross-country sprint event in Tesero, Italy, on Tuesday. Silver medallist Linn Kazmaier of Germany and her guide Florian Baumann turned their backs on the Russian pair on the podium when the anthem was played. The pair also stood away from Bagiian and Siniakin when photos were taken, protesting the inclusion of Russian athletes at these Games, the first time they have competed at a Winter Paralympics under their own flag since 2014.

Kazmaier explained their decision to German broadcaster ARD: “I don’t ‌know ⁠these people, maybe they don’t support the system in Russia either. Maybe they are really nice people who we could actually be friends with. But it’s such a shame that politics overshadows everything. So we decided to keep our hats on and ​not turn towards the ​flags, because we ⁠don’t support that.”

Baumann added that they wanted to show solidarity with Ukrainian athletes whom they met in Beijing at the last winter Games four years ago. Russia first invaded Ukraine in 2014 when it annexed Crimea, and launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

IPC rules prevent athletes from “any demonstration, protest, political statement or similar conduct (which) hinders or disrupts competitions or official ceremonies, including medal ceremonies.” What the IPC consider to be protests are strictly prohibited from the field of play, which extends beyond the cross-country course to include the podium, anti-doping testing spaces, storage areas and athlete lounges.

The Paralympic organisation said in a statement to The Athletic: “We are aware of the matter, are gathering evidence and analysing it.”

The German Paralympic Committee has been approached for comment.

This is already the second instance of issues with athletes at cross-country podiums at the Milan-Cortina Games. Ukrainian biathlete Oleksandra Kononova wore earrings which featured Ukraine colours and the words “STOP WAR” when she won gold in the women’s individual standing category on Saturday. She was subsequently warned for this and IPC officials demanded she hand take them off and hand them over before receiving her medal. The Ukraine NPC say she removed them but did not give them to officials.

“All people in the world today want to stop the war,” Valerii Sushkevych, the president of the Ukrainian National Paralympic, told The Athletic over a video call. “This lady, a Paralympic champion, is a mother of two daughters. She wants to stop the war,” he added, calling the IPC’s decisions “terrible.”

Six Russian athletes, as well as four Belarusian athletes, are competing at these Games because they were awarded “bipartite” entries. These were automatic qualifications — officially confirmed less than two weeks before the start of the Paralympics — for specific top-level athletes. IPC members voted last September to lift the ban on Russia and Belarus, however, sport-specific governing bodies did not permit them in qualifying. Only when Russia and Belarus, separately, took FIS (the international ski and snowboard federation) to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in December 2025, did their competing in Italy become possible.

Their exclusion was overturned on discrimination grounds and, without what CAS called a “framework” for competing under neutral terms, Russian and Belarusian athletes were permitted, as were their flags and national anthems. Consequently, seven European countries, including Ukraine, boycotted last Friday’s opening ceremony.

At the opening ceremony, IPC President Andrew Parsons said: “Four years ago, I said I was horrified at what was happening in the world. Unfortunately, the situation has not improved. In a world where some countries are better known by the names of their leaders, I prefer to know countries by the name of their athletes. Sport offers the world another way forward, another perspective.”

Russia currently ranks joint-fourth on the medal table with Austria, winning six medals total, with four golds and two bronze medals. Bagiian also took gold in the women’s 10km interval start classic, while Ivan Golubkov finished first in the men’s sitting classification of the same event. In alpine, Varvara Voronchikhina claimed super-G gold, and her and Aleksei Bugaev both took bronze in the standing downhill races.
